newsitem.title: MEXICO: Economists, markets welcome Mexico 1997 budget.
newsitem.headline: Economists, markets welcome Mexico 1997 budget.

text.p: Economists on Friday welcomed Mexico's 1997 budget proposals as a realistic blueprint for economic recovery that juggles demands for fiscal restraint with the pressing need for more growth.

The budget, presented on Thursday to Congress by Mexican Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz, calls for a slight budget deficit to make up for what has been a slower-than-expected recovery by recession-weary consumers.

"The budget removes any lingering uncertainty about economic policy next year and shows the government is gradually placing more emphasis on growth," said Damian Fraser, director of Caspian Research in Mexico City.
Mexico's financial markets gave a warm welcome to the budget on Friday. Stocks rallied 1.65 percent and the peso gained slightly against the dollar.
Despite heavy spending pressures, Mexico should have no problem meeting its target of a slight budget deficit equalling 0.5 percent of GDP, economists said.
Some assumptions in the budget are probably too optimistic, such as an estimated 10 percent real growth in tax receipts, economists said.
But most are realistic or conservative, such as a projected $14.50 per barrel in oil revenues compared to current oil prices of about $18 per barrel.

"The $14.50 per barrel is conservative even if a drop in the price of oil is expected for next year ... thus, the government is reducing the risk of not reaching its budget," said Santander Investment economists Hector Chavez and Enrique Ramirez in a report.
Fraser said the government can always cut back on spending if its revenues fall short of budget targets, although it is unlikely to cut spending ahead of July's mid-term elections.
"In general terms Mexico has always delivered fairly well on its budget numbers," he said.
The budget calls for four percent economic growth next year, nearly all of which will come from investment and consumption. Exports will add only a fraction to growth.
Although private consumption is an important part of the growth equation, the government forecast it will grow by just 2.4 percent in real terms.
